third-party list mid-run is neither deterministic nor self-contained, and
the handout requires the marketplace manifest to resolve with no external
Bot names churn. Both the snapshot date and the upstream commit are printed
in every report so a reader can judge how stale this list is, and re-derive
The three-way classification is ours, not upstream's. Upstream lists bots to
block; we need to know what blocking each one COSTS, which is a different
question and the reason a flat list produces bad findings.

source.note: Bot names cross-checked against this snapshot; the retrieval/training/dual-purpose classification is this marketplace's own work and is not asserted by upstream.

retrieval.meaning: Fetches pages at answer time to ground or cite a response. Blocking one of these removes the brand from that assistant's answers.

training.meaning: Collects content for model training corpora. Blocking has no effect on whether the brand is retrieved or cited at answer time.

dual_purpose.meaning: Contested. Vendor documentation ties the token to more than one use, or the vendor has changed its stated scope. Blocking may or may not cost retrieval visibility.

Contested. Google documents this token as controlling whether content helps improve Gemini apps and grounded answers. It is not a crawler in its own right - it modifies how Googlebot-crawled content may be used - so blocking it does not remove the site from Google Search, but it can affect AI-surface grounding. Report as a trade-off the site may have chosen deliberately, never as an error.

crawl_delay_honoured_by._comment: Crawl-delay is NOT part of RFC 9309. Which crawlers honour it decides whether setting one is a mistake or a deliberate, effective choice.
crawl_delay_honoured_by.note: Google documents that Googlebot ignores Crawl-delay and that crawl rate is managed in Search Console instead. A site that sets Crawl-delay for Bingbot has made a supported, effective choice and must not be reported as having made a mistake.
